Welcome toRandom Walk on a Line

Two thousand walkers start together and step left or right at random — then what?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: a crowd of random walkers on a line

Source

Concept
A one-dimensional random walk: 2000 independent walkers start at the origin and, once every time interval τ, each steps a distance ℓ to the right or to the left with probability 1/2 each. A steady walker starts at the same place and steps to the right every time.
Serves
Measuring how the crowd's mean position ⟨x⟩, mean square displacement ⟨x²⟩ and root-mean-square distance xrms = √⟨x²⟩ depend on the time, the step length ℓ and the time per step τ, and comparing them with the steady walker.
On screen
A fixed x axis from −120 to +120 µm. Above it, 21 rows: the steady walker (red, top row) and the first twenty walkers of the crowd, each hopping at every step. Below, a histogram of all 2000 walkers with bins 2ℓ wide centred on the sites (2n − N)ℓ that can be occupied after N steps; bar height is the fraction of walkers in the bin. A companion plot records distance from the origin against time for the crowd and the steady walker.
Timing
Simulated time runs at 10 ms per second of real time at 1× speed. A run lasts 200 ms, pauses by itself at 50, 100 and 150 ms; Run again, or changing ℓ or τ, restarts it. Every run draws fresh random steps.
Inquiry
Five gated questions, each checked by running the walk and reading the histogram and the Readouts panel below the controls, then a closing summary card.
Misconception
The alternative choices in each question encode intuitions students commonly bring to this problem; they are addressed in the feedback only after a choice is made.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit before observingEach question is gated: the student commits to an answer, then checks it in the sim; when a question opens the run is returned to t = 0 and paused, so its outcome is not yet on screen.
Staged, purposeful numbersThe Readouts panel shows only the two quantities the current question uses; the distance–time plot and the dashed ± rms marks on the histogram appear with xrms. After the last question all six readouts and the plot stay on.
Real values, honestly labelledStep length in µm and time per step in ms; the slowed clock (10 ms of simulated time per second of real time at 1×) is printed on the scene.
Stable scalesThe x axis (−120 to +120 µm), the fraction axis (0 to 0.30) and the plot axes (0 to 200 ms, 0 to 30 µm) never rescale; bars above 0.30 are cut with a break mark, and a walker beyond the axis becomes an arrow at the end of its row.
Honest randomnessEvery run draws fresh random steps for 2000 walkers, so the readouts scatter by a few per cent from run to run.
Misconceptions addressed structurallyAlternative intuitions appear only as answer choices, each with its own feedback after a choice is made, never as standing text.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Watching the crowd

Keep ℓ = 1.0 µm and τ = 1.0 ms and press play, letting the run continue past each pause to 200 ms while watching the histogram, the twenty rows and the readout ⟨x⟩. What happens to the crowd?

2 · Walkers at the origin

Press play and let the run pause by itself at t = 50 ms, when N = 50. Look at the bar at x = 0 in the histogram. What fraction of the walkers is standing exactly at the origin?

3 · Four times as long

Press play with ℓ = 1.0 µm and τ = 1.0 ms. At the pause at t = 50 ms read xrms and xs, then continue to the end of the run at t = 200 ms, four times as long, and read them again. How do they change?

4 · Longer steps

Set ℓ = 1.5 µm (the 1.5 chip does it), keep τ = 1.0 ms, and press play. At the pause at t = 100 ms, when N = 100, what does the readout ⟨x²⟩ show?

5 · Same speed, longer steps

Return to ℓ = 1.0 µm and τ = 1.0 ms, where the run ends with xrms at about 14.1 µm and xs at 200 µm. Now set ℓ = 2.0 µm and τ = 2.0 ms, so that the steady walker keeps the same speed ℓ/τ, and run to the end at t = 200 ms. What does xrms read?

6 · Spreading by random steps

A crowd of random walkers keeps its mean at the origin while it spreads: ⟨x⟩ = 0, but ⟨x²⟩ = Nℓ² = (ℓ²/τ) t. So the rms distance grows as √t, ever more slowly than the steady walker's distance (ℓ/τ) t.

How fast a crowd spreads is set by ℓ²/τ, not by the speed ℓ/τ. This is diffusion: ⟨x²⟩ = 2Dt, with the diffusion coefficient D = ℓ²/2τ in one dimension. For a gas molecule ℓ²/τ = v̄λ, so this agrees with the notes' D = ⅓v̄λ up to a numerical factor.

A Crowd of Random Walkers

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A crowd of 2000 walkers starts together at the origin of a line. Once every time interval τ, each steps a distance ℓ to the right or to the left, with equal chance. A steady walker steps right every time. The sim follows how far each kind gets.

What you'll learn

  • What the twenty rows, the histogram and the readouts show.
  • How ⟨x²⟩ and xrms depend on the number of steps N, the step length ℓ and the time per step τ.
  • How the crowd's distance compares with the steady walker's.
The set-up: every walker at the origin, before the first step.

What's on screen

  • White dots: the first twenty walkers of the crowd, one per row, hopping at each step.
  • Red: the steady walker, in the top row and in the lower plot.
  • Blue bars: all 2000 walkers. Bar height is the fraction of the crowd on that site.
  • Dashed lines: ±xrms, where xrms = √⟨x²⟩ is the rms distance of the crowd from the origin.
  • Readouts: t, N, ⟨x⟩, ⟨x²⟩, xrms and xs, the steady walker's position.
See itPlay a run at your current settings. Watch for: the twenty rows hopping, the histogram filling in, and the run pausing itself at 50 ms.

03

The mean position stays at zero

A walker that takes N steps, n of them to the right and N − n to the left, ends at x = (2n − N)ℓ (notes 4.5). Right and left are equally likely, so the mean of n is N/2 and the mean position is ⟨x⟩ = 0 at every time. This follows from the symmetry of the two directions alone.

x = (2n − N)ℓ   ⟨x⟩ = 0
Notes (4.5).

So the crowd stays centred on the origin however many steps are taken. A single walker does not average out, but 2000 walkers nearly do: the readout ⟨x⟩ scatters about zero by roughly xrms/√2000, which is 0.3 µm at 200 ms.

The expected histogram after N = 50 steps. The sim's own bars scatter a little around this shape.
See itThe sim plays three runs to 200 ms. Watch for: the ⟨x⟩ readout landing within a few tenths of a micrometre of zero each time, on either side.
04

Few walkers are back at the origin

A walker stands on x = 0 only if exactly half its N steps went to the right, so n = N/2. The chance is the binomial probability for N even.

P(x = 0) = N! / [(N/2)!]2 · 2−N

At N = 50 it is 0.112, so about 224 of the 2000 walkers stand on the origin, not half of them. This is the tallest bar in the histogram. The chance keeps falling as N grows, in line with the 1/√N fall of the peak in the notes' Figure 25: 0.080 at N = 100 and 0.056 at N = 200. After an odd number of steps nobody stands on x = 0, because the sites (2n − N)ℓ are then odd multiples of ℓ.

The exact chance of standing on the origin, for even N.
See itThe sim jumps to the pause at 50 ms, where N = 50. Watch for: the bar at x = 0 reaching about 0.11 on the fraction axis, the tallest bar and far below one half.
05

The mean square grows with N

Each step adds ±ℓ to x. The variance of x is 4ℓ2 times the variance of n, and for equal chances the variance of n is N/4, so the mean square displacement grows by ℓ2 per step (notes 4.6). Squares are never negative, so they do not cancel the way the signed steps do.

⟨x2⟩ = Nℓ2   xrms = √N  ℓ
Notes (4.6).

At ℓ = 1.5 µm and N = 100, ⟨x2⟩ = 100 × 2.25 = 225 µm2 and xrms = 15.0 µm. That is Nℓ2, not Nℓ = 150 and not (Nℓ)2 = 22 500 µm2, which is the square of the steady walker's distance xs = Nℓ = 150 µm.

⟨x2⟩ = Nℓ2 for three step lengths.
See itThe sim jumps to ℓ = 1.5 µm, τ = 1.0 ms and the pause at 100 ms. Watch for: the ⟨x²⟩ readout near 225 µm², with a few per cent of random scatter.
06

In a time t the rms distance grows as √t

If one step is taken in every interval τ, then N = t/τ and the mean square becomes proportional to the time (notes 4.7). The rms distance therefore grows only as √t, while the steady walker, who always steps right, covers xs = Nℓ = (ℓ/τ) t, which is proportional to t itself.

⟨x2⟩ = (ℓ2/τ) t   xrms = ℓ√(t/τ)
Notes (4.7).

At ℓ = τ = 1 the run pauses at 50, 100 and 150 ms and ends at 200 ms. Between the first pause and the end the time is multiplied by four. So xs goes from 50 to 200 µm and ⟨x2⟩ from 50 to 200 µm2, but xrms, the square root, only doubles: from 7.1 to 14.1 µm.

ℓ = τ = 1Nxs (µm)⟨x2⟩ (µm2)xrms (µm)
t = 50 ms5050507.1
t = 100 ms10010010010.0
t = 150 ms15015015012.2
t = 200 ms20020020014.1
The sim's distance plot at ℓ = τ = 1: the steady walker leaves the 30 µm axis at 30 ms.
See itThe sim jumps to 50 ms, then to 200 ms, at ℓ = τ = 1. Watch for: xs going from 50 to 200 µm while xrms only goes from about 7 to about 14 µm.
07

The same speed can spread the crowd differently

The steady walker's speed is ℓ/τ, but the crowd's spreading is set by ℓ2/τ. Doubling both ℓ and τ leaves ℓ/τ = 1 µm/ms, so xs at 200 ms is still 200 µm. The number of steps halves, to 100, yet ℓ2/τ doubles from 1 to 2 µm2/ms. So ⟨x2⟩ goes from 200 to 400 µm2 and xrms from 14.1 to 20.0 µm.

xs = (ℓ/τ) t   ⟨x2⟩ = (ℓ2/τ) t

Half as many steps, each twice as long, is not a wash: each step counts ℓ2, so the longer steps win.

ℓ = 1, τ = 12001.01.020014.1
ℓ = 2, τ = 21001.02.020020.0
ℓ = 2, τ = 12002.04.040028.3
ℓ = 1, τ = 21000.50.510010.0

08

Where it matters

  • Diffusion. The combination ℓ2/τ has the dimensions of the diffusion coefficient D in Fick's law. For a gas molecule ℓ is the mean free path λ and λ = v̄τ, so ℓ2/τ = v̄λ. The notes find D = ⅓ v̄λ (Section 1.4): the same product, up to a numerical factor that a walk in one dimension cannot get right.
  • Averages over many particles. The scatter of a crowd average falls as 1/√N, which is why the pressure of a gas does not visibly fluctuate (notes, Section 4.1).
  • The binomial distribution. The histogram here is the distribution of the notes' Figure 25, which also counts objects in two states.
Go deeper: why the readouts sit near the formulas, not on them

The readouts average over a sample of 2000 walkers. For many steps the scatter of ⟨x2⟩ is about √(2/2000) = 3% of its value, so at 200 ms it reads 200 ± 6 µm2. Run again draws fresh steps. The steady walker has no random steps, so xs = Nℓ is exact.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim sends 2000 walkers off a line, each stepping ±ℓ every τ, and shows ⟨x⟩, ⟨x2⟩ and xrms for the crowd beside xs for a walker who always steps right.

Key points

  • ⟨x⟩ = 0 at every time, but ⟨x2⟩ = Nℓ2 = (ℓ2/τ) t.
  • xrms grows as √t; the steady walker's xs grows as t.
  • The crowd's spreading is set by ℓ2/τ, not by the speed ℓ/τ.

Common mix-ups

  • “The crowd stays bunched at the origin, because left and right cancel.” They cancel in ⟨x⟩, not in ⟨x2⟩. At 200 ms xrms = 14.1 µm.
  • “After 50 steps about half the walkers are back at the origin.” Only those with exactly 25 steps to the right: 0.112 of them.
  • “The same speed ℓ/τ means the same xrms.” At ℓ = τ = 2 the speed is unchanged and xrms at 200 ms is 20.0 µm, not 14.1.

Things to try on your own

  • At ℓ = τ = 1, read xrms at each pause and check that its square matches N.
  • Compare ℓ = 2, τ = 1 with ℓ = 1, τ = 2 at 200 ms.
  • Press Run again several times and watch ⟨x⟩ scatter about zero.
